title: install-liveness-deadlock-hypotheses-fast-remediation-playbook
content:
Purpose
-----
This is a rapid-response playbook for common liveness/deadlock symptoms observed during install and early runtime on VPC/on‑prem private deployments. It focuses on hypothesis-driven probes you can run with a phone-and-terminal workflow, quick mitigations to get the cluster back to serving, and safe rollback steps for Terraform-driven installs.

Audience and scope
------------------
- Primary: SREs and first‑line support for private deployments (onprem + VPC).
- Secondary: infra engineers and field SEs doing upgrades or customer smoke tests.
- Not covered: deep kernel debugging, hardware RMA procedures (link to HW runbook in Confluence).

When to use this doc
--------------------
Start here when new install or post‑upgrade cluster shows:
- Pods stuck in CrashLoopBackOff or ContainerCreating for >5–10m
- API server unresponsive or times out often
- High CPU spin on control plane or serving nodes, but low request throughput
- Tokenized model processes appear to hang (long latencies, repeated timeouts)

Quick triage (phone-and-terminal)
--------------------------------
1) Slack/phone: inform oncall, post one‑line symptom + cluster name.
2) Get a k8s context and node list: kubectl get nodes -o wide --context=<ctx>
3) Check control plane health: kubectl get --raw='/readyz' || curl -sS --fail http://<apiserver>:6443/readyz
4) Are pods scheduling? kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase!=Running
5) Look for imagepullbackoff or pvc mount errors first. kubectl describe pod <pod>

Fast signal map (what a probe tells you)
--------------------------------------
- ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull => registry auth or network egress (check NAT/GW rules).
- ContainerCreating + attach/mount timeouts => PV/Cinder/NFS/Ceph issues or slow host disk I/O.
- CrashLoopBackOff with OOMKilled => memory pressure or bad init args.
- Node NotReady + kubelet flapping => kernel panics, cgroup issues, or kubelet config mismatch after upgrade.
- High steady CPU on gRPC worker processes with low socket throughput => thread starvation / lock contention (see golang pprof notes below).

Fast commands (copy/paste)
-------------------------
- node health: kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status}{"\n"}{end}'
- kubelet logs (recent): journalctl -u kubelet -n 500 --no-pager
- docker/containerd list: ps -eo pid,cmd | egrep 'containerd|dockerd'
- kernel OOM logs: journalctl -k | egrep -i 'oom|killed process' -B3 -A3
- dmesg recent: dmesg --ctime | tail -n 200
- disk I/O saturation: iostat -xz 1 5 or sar -d 1 5
- NVMe SMART: sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0n1
- GPU: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=temperature.gpu,utilization.gpu,memory.used --format=csv,noheader,nounits

Common hypotheses and tests
--------------------------
1) Network egress blocked by customer firewall (image pulls, license checks fail)
   - Test: curl -v https://ghcr.io/v2/ || curl -v https://registry-1.docker.io/v2/ from a node.
   - Quick fix: add temporary NAT rule or proxy, re-run kubectl rollout restart daemonset/whatever.

2) PVC mount timeouts due to NFS/CIFS load or misconfigured StorageClass
   - Test: ls -l /var/lib/kubelet/pods/<podUID>/volumes; check kubelet logs for mount errors.
   - Quick fix: switch to alternative StorageClass for the pod (if available), or scale down other I/O heavy workloads.

3) Kubelet/node config drift after upgrade (cgroup driver mismatch, kubelet flags changed)
   - Test: compare /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml to backed up config (we keep /var/backups/kubelet/config.yaml on-provision).
   - Quick fix: revert kubelet flags to previous known good config, systemctl restart kubelet.

4) Process deadlock in runtime (KV cache locks, global mutex)
   - Test: capture pprof/profile endpoint (if enabled) or strace -p <pid> for 30s to look for repeated futex syscalls.
   - Quick fix: restart the offending process/pod; if happens frequently, mark node unschedulable and cordon + drain.

Terraform module quick notes (what to check)
-------------------------------------------
- State drift: terraform plan can be misleading if remote state is out of date. Always run terraform refresh before plan in an incident.
- Provider versions: check versions.tf for provider lock; mismatch commonly causes subtle behavior change in cloud provider resources (routes, NAT gateway).
- IAM role scoping: install failures showing 403 or forbidden usually due to assumed role missing policies; check module variable overrides for iam_role_arn.
- Security group/cidr assumptions: customer VPCs sometimes have narrower egress rules than expected; validate the managed-egress rules in network module.
- Wait-for resources: add explicit null_resource/local-exec checks (sleepy wait) in the module that handles onprem bootstrap for eventual consistency with DNS or BGP.

Preflight checks before any upgrade (fast checklist)
--------------------------------------------------
- Have a terraform plan and a plan artifact in GH. Upload plan to incident channel.
- Verify canaries: deploy a smoke canary set (model-echo small pod) to verify inference path before full rollout.
- Disk usage on nodes: df -h and du -sh /var/lib/docker /var/lib/kubelet. <80% recommended.
- Time sync: chrony/ntpctl sources healthy. Clock drift > 500ms => certs and TLS connections flakey.
- Kernel/config compatibility: kubelet and docker/containerd expected versions matrix exists in Confluence.

Safe rollback (Terraform-centric)
--------------------------------
- If upgrade included infra changes (tf apply) that affect networking/storage, do NOT plan immediate full destroy. Use terraform apply with old module versions + targeted resource replacements where possible.
- Typical safe rollback steps: 1) terraform apply -var-file=known-good.tfvars -target=module.network 2) Wait for network routes and NAT state to converge 3) rolling-restart control plane nodes 4) re-run smoke canary.
- If the state file was overwritten by a failed apply, escalate to infra-engineering. Do not manually edit remote state unless instructed.

Hotfixes and micro-remediations (fast to apply)
-----------------------------------------------
- kube-proxy churn: restart kube-proxy daemonset one node at a time to clear conntrack overload.
- conntrack table full: sudo sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max; echo <bigger> | sudo tee /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max. (Warn: increases memory usage.)
- aggressive OOM events: add temporary eviction thresholds via kubelet flags or taint/evict the noisy pod.
- slow image pulls: pre-pull images on nodes with crictl pull <image> and restart pod.

Observability pointers (what to collect for postmortem)
------------------------------------------------------
- kubectl get events -A --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' > events-<ts>.txt
- node-level top/jstack snapshots from each affected node (top -b -n1; for Java processes use jstack)
- pprof/profile dumps from runtime (CPU, heap) and corresponding pod logs for the 5 min window around the first error.
- terraform plan + state snapshot and TF logs (apply output).

Escalation matrix
-----------------
- Oncall SRE (first 30m): triage network/registry and do hotfixes above.
- Eng-private-deployments lead (30–90m): run terraform refresh/plan, decide canary rollback.
- Serving-runtime / Applied-ML (90m+): investigate runtime deadlock patterns and mitigation via config flags (e.g., kv_cache.enable_shard=true).
- Infra (if remote state or provider issues): do not attempt manual state surgery without infra signoff.

Remediation templates (copy into Slack incident)
------------------------------------------------
- Short status update: "Cluster <name>: elevated pod crash rate after upgrade; blocked on PVC mounts and kubelet errors. Running node-level IO checks and attempting temporary StorageClass fallback. ETA 60m."
- Action to run (example): "On node node-05, run: sudo systemctl restart kubelet && journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 --no-pager > /tmp/kubelet-log-node05.txt"

Notes-to-self / Unresolved questions
----------------------------------
- Consider adding a tiny watchdog sidecar to model workers to emit liveness metrics (locks held count, goroutine stacks) on /debug for easier triage.
- Should we include an opt-in conntrack tuning step in the default TF module for onprem? Customer envs vary — needs opt-out semantics.
- Add an emergency tf var to skip storage class provisioning when operator prefers manual LVM/Nimble.

Appendix: quick golang deadlock probe
------------------------------------
- If process has pprof endpoint: curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2 > goroutines.txt and inspect blocked goroutines / repeated stack frames.
- If no pprof, strace -f -p <pid> -o /tmp/strace.out for 20s and look for repeated futex/wait syscalls.
- If you suspect lock contention, restart one replica at a time and watch latency curves (reduce blast radius).

References and further reading
-----------------------------
- internal: private-deploys/troubleshooting-index (Confluence)
- internal: GH PRs and TF modules referenced above
- external: linux conntrack tuning guides, Kubernetes eviction docs

Last updated notes
------------------
- Drafted by Priya Nair; collabs: Miguel, Sofia, Ethan. Use this as a quick-first-run checklist for field incidents; move items into runbooks as we confirm reliability improvements.
